desc: Guru's measured rhymes over DJ Premier's chopped jazz and soul samples and scratched hooks.
Rock band remade by Andrew Weatherall's production into a fusion of acid house, gospel and psychedelia.
Sample-based debut mixing house beats, sixties pop and London atmosphere with Sarah Cracknell's light vocals.
Ice-T's hard-edged street narratives, including the debut of his metal band Body Count.
Rick Rubin-produced album balancing tight funk grooves with introspective ballads, recorded in a mansion.
Debut built on DJ Muggs's murky, bass-heavy beats and B-Real's nasal, cannabis-themed delivery.
The Black Album: slower, streamlined heavy metal with huge production by Bob Rock.
Long, eco-political psychedelic rock album mixing funk grooves, garage rock and spiritual themes.
French-language debut pairing MC Solaar's wordplay with jazzy, laid-back beats.
Debut of soaring guitar rock and Eddie Vedder's baritone, centred on stories of trauma and alienation.
Dense, noisy political rap from Chuck D and Flavor Flav, including a remake with Anthrax.
Fast, precise thrash with death metal heaviness and early hints of Brazilian percussion.
Kevin Shields's layered, pitch-bending guitar walls with buried, breathy vocals and sampled textures.
Quiet-loud guitar pieces with murmured narratives that became a template for post-rock.
Butch Vig-produced album of pop hooks inside loud-quiet grunge that took alternative rock mainstream.
Minimal beats built on jazz basslines with Q-Tip and Phife Dawg trading conversational verses.
Piano-led debut of confessional songs about faith, sexuality and trauma.
Long Sufi devotional performances where Nusrat's improvising voice builds over harmonium and handclaps.
British hip hop and dance crossover with funky grooves, soulful backing vocals and catchy hooks.
Stripped trio debut of jagged blues-rock guitar and Polly Harvey's forceful voice.
Short collection of compact, melodic guitar-pop songs sung in Evan Dando's relaxed baritone.
Lang's move from country to lush torch songs about longing.
Afrocentric, socially conscious rap with Southern blues and gospel influences and a warm, communal feel.
Subdued, mostly acoustic songs about mortality and memory, with string arrangements by John Paul Jones.
Soukous from Koffi Olomide with chiming electric guitars and danceable rhythms.
Loud, guitar-driven set of violent, biblical-toned story songs.
Scrappy, lo-fi debut mixing hissy guitar noise, tunes and Stephen Malkmus's oblique lyrics.
Mick Ronson-produced album of loud glam and rockabilly guitars with Morrissey's arch lyrics.
Baaba Maal's high voice over Senegalese drumming and modern production, rooted in Fulani tradition.
Bob Mould's post-Hüsker Dü trio combining heavy guitar distortion with strong pop melodies.
Butch Vig-produced album pairing noisy guitar textures with tighter, grunge-era song structures.
Alex Chilton's frayed, unsettling songs, recorded in 1974 and released years later.
Pounding industrial metal of sequenced beats, thrash guitars, samples and distorted vocals.
Michael Franti's political rap over industrial and jazz-inflected beats, covering media, war and race.
Debut of droning, slowly building space rock with gauzy vocals and layered guitars and keyboards.
Groove metal of mid-tempo riffs, hard-hitting drums and shouted vocals.
Comic, irreverent debut over jazzy beats from producer J-Swift.
Lo-fi early recordings by Richard D. James blending soft analogue melodies with gentle techno beats.
Debut built on slow P-Funk-derived grooves and whiny synth leads, introducing Snoop Doggy Dogg.
Ice Cube's angry response to the 1992 Los Angeles unrest, mixed with lighter, more celebratory tracks.
Clanking, percussive songs about death and decay, sung in Waits's rasp.
Sludgy riffs and layered vocal harmonies on songs about addiction and despair.
Political rap-rock with Zack de la Rocha's shouted verses and Tom Morello's effects-driven guitar.
Luke Haines's debut of literate, sardonic guitar songs with glam touches and cello.
Loose, rootsy debut that grew out of informal Los Angeles studio sessions.
Bright, heavily produced synth-pop with dance beats and Neil Tennant's wry, personal lyrics.
Debut of glam guitar and Brett Anderson's theatrical vocals about suburban sex and seediness.
Debut of brooding, atmospheric Americana led by Grant-Lee Phillips's high, emotive voice.
Twin-bass post-hardcore with a dark, sleazy groove and half-spoken vocals.
Aimee Mann's solo debut of sharp, melodic songs about disappointment and the music industry.
Weller's rootsy record of pastoral folk-rock and soulful jams.
Jay Kay's debut of acid jazz with seventies funk grooves, didgeridoo and environmental themes.
Sparse, frank guitar songs about sex and relationships, framed as a reply to Exile on Main St.
Blur's turn to quintessentially English guitar pop, observing London life and suburban boredom.
Greg Dulli's dark, soul-tinged songs about obsession and failing relationships.
Mark E. Smith's barbed, repetitive post-punk with a cleaner, poppier production.
Steve Albini-recorded album of abrasive, dynamic songs and harsh, unvarnished production.
Ambitious psychedelic pop moving between shoegaze noise, dub, horns and Beatles-like melodies.
The Hartnoll brothers' long, building techno tracks with melodic synth layers.
Instrumental electronic album of atmospheric downtempo textures.
Lo-fi indie rock moving between raw breakup songs and noisy guitar rock.
Dr. Dre-produced debut of slow G-funk grooves under Snoop's relaxed, drawling flow.
Densely overdubbed guitar walls and soft, nostalgic passages, produced by Butch Vig.
Björk's solo debut mixing club beats, jazz standards and Icelandic quirks, produced by Nellee Hooper.
RZA's raw, murky beats and kung fu samples behind nine distinct MCs.
Steve Albini-recorded follow-up, rawer and more abrasive than Nevermind.
Costello reunited with most of the Attractions for punchy, wordy new wave rock.
Fast, hook-filled pop punk about boredom, anxiety and slacking that broke the band into the mainstream.
Debut blending acoustic blues guitar and harmonica with hip hop rhythms and relaxed vocals.
Trent Reznor's concept album of self-destruction built from abrasive electronics and fragile piano moments.
Cleaner, more melodic follow-up of loose, tuneful guitar songs and oblique lyrics.
Slow, bass-heavy trip hop with guest vocalists including Tracey Thorn, Tricky and Horace Andy.
Former Pixies leader's long, eclectic solo album of catchy guitar songs and surreal lyrics.
Sweeping, orchestrated album of dark ballads and glam rock, Bernard Butler's last with the band.
Dark, angular rock with Richey Edwards's lyrics on atrocity, self-harm and political horror.
Beth Gibbons's sorrowful vocals over vinyl crackle, spy-film samples and slow breakbeats.
Collaboration with Ry Cooder linking Malian guitar traditions and American blues.
Loud, guitar-heavy debut of big choruses, working-class escapism and Liam Gallagher's sneering vocals.
Andrew Weatherall's dub-heavy instrumental electronica, conceived as a soundtrack for an imagined film.
High-energy rave and breakbeat album responding to UK laws restricting raves and free parties.
Character sketches of English life in styles ranging from disco and music hall to punk.
Jeff Buckley's only studio album, showcasing his wide-ranging voice on originals and covers.
Darker, socially critical concept album of shifting techno, ambient and drum and bass textures.
Heavy, psychedelic grunge with alternate guitar tunings and Chris Cornell's powerful voice.
Jeru's debut over sparse, eerie DJ Premier beats.
Wu-Tang member's solo debut over RZA's dark, dusty production.
Steve Lillywhite-produced record of introspective, graceful songs.
Trio's R&B blend of smooth ballads, hip hop beats and rap verses.
Mixes rap, jazzy funk instrumentals and short hardcore punk blasts.
Nas's detailed portraits of Queensbridge life over jazz-tinged beats from Premier, Pete Rock and Large Professor.
Courtney Love's screamed and sung songs about femininity, violence and motherhood over loud guitars.
Long, intricate post-hardcore songs with interlocking guitars and screamed vocals.
Biggie's debut of vivid Brooklyn street storytelling, from struggle and crime to fame and despair.
Acoustic live set with cello, favouring covers of Meat Puppets, Lead Belly and Bowie.
Fast, catchy skate punk that sold millions on an independent label.
D'Angelo's debut fusing classic soul, jazz chords and hip hop rhythms.
Psychedelic guitar rock with long, swirling jams and Richard Ashcroft's yearning vocals.
Debut largely written and played by Dave Grohl, mixing loud punk energy with pop melodies.
Tricky's murmured vocals alongside Martina Topley-Bird over dense, smoky beats and unsettling samples.
Twenty-eight brief, home-recorded pop fragments with hissy fidelity and British Invasion melodies.
Fela's son updating Afrobeat with tighter, punchier songs, horn riffs and political themes.
Jarvis Cocker's sharp vignettes about class, sex and nightlife set to glam, disco-tinged pop.
Short, sharp guitar songs drawing on Wire and late-seventies new wave.
Debut of energetic, youthful guitar pop with punk speed and sixties melodies.
2Pac's introspective set about paranoia, mortality and family, released while he was in prison.
Layered, guitar-driven rock with Thom Yorke's falsetto and themes of alienation and illness.
Long, orchestral drum and bass album fusing jungle breakbeats with jazz and soul textures.
Garage punk with horns, fifties rock and roll swagger and big singalong choruses.
Raekwon and Ghostface's crime narratives over RZA's cinematic, soul-sampling production.
Mostly instrumental downtempo album of slow hip hop beats, warm basslines and smoky atmosphere.
Oasis's best-selling second album of big singalong anthems and ballads.
GZA's precise, chess-like lyricism over RZA's bleak beats and samurai film dialogue.
Debut of distorted breakbeats, acid squelches and psychedelic samples that defined big beat.
Shirley Manson fronting slick, sample-heavy alternative rock produced by Butch Vig and bandmates.
Progressive house album with dub basslines and guest vocalists including John Lydon.
Two-disc album moving from metallic rock to piano ballads, themed around life and death.
Raw, emotionally direct songs of anger and introspection that became one of the decade's best sellers.
Teenage Northern Irish trio's debut of fast, catchy guitar songs about summer and love.
Double album expanding alt-country into rootsy rock, pop and loose studio experiments.
Blend of hip hop, rock, funk and lounge with half-spoken vocals.
Lush, orchestral rock anthems recorded after the disappearance of Richey Edwards.
Polished Swedish indie pop pairing Nina Persson's sweet vocals with darker lyrics.
Concept album about a love affair, built on falsetto vocals and live seventies-style soul grooves.
Bass-less trio's raw, scuzzy blues-punk with hollered vocals and noisy guitar.
Stuart Murdoch's soft-voiced, literate pop songs about misfits, religion and Glasgow life.
Trent Reznor co-produced concept rock opera of abrasive industrial metal.
E's debut of lo-fi samples and catchy alternative rock about loneliness and odd characters.
Kool Keith's surreal sci-fi rhymes over Dan the Automator's eerie beats.
Motorik grooves, vintage keyboards and French and English vocals, with jazzy, retro-futurist arrangements.
Mix compilation of smooth, jazzy drum and bass with atmospheric pads and rolling breakbeats.
Downtuned groove metal fused with Brazilian percussion, recorded partly with the Xavante people.
Tracey Thorn's cool vocals over trip hop and drum and bass rhythms from Ben Watt.
Neil Hannon's orchestral pop about seduction and decadence, sung in a Scott Walker-like croon.
Mark Lanegan's dark baritone over psychedelic, sixties-influenced grunge.
Debut of eccentric, melodic guitar pop with psychedelic and glam touches and surreal lyrics.
Norman Cook's debut as Fatboy Slim of sampled breakbeats, acid squelches and hooky loops.
Instrumental post-rock with an extended opening suite, built on dub bass, vibraphone and krautrock rhythm.
Dust Brothers-produced collage of folk, funk, hip hop and rock built on samples and live playing.
